title: Final Decision C26-0010 2024FT46 TOPAZE Z Martin Andrade
text:
DECISION of the FEI TRIBUNAL
10 August 2026
In the matter of
Mr Martín Andrade (PR; Ref. C26-0010)
(FEI Case number: FEI 2024/FT46 – TOPAZE Z)
FEI Tribunal Hearing Panel: Mr Agustín Fattal Jaef (ARG)
FEI Tribunal Reference: C26-0010 [FEI 2024/FT46 – TOPAZE Z]
Person Responsible/ID/NF: Martín Andrade / 10154649 / ECU
Horse/Passport/NF: TOPAZE Z / 107HR30 / ECU
Event/ID: CH-S.Am-J-S – Quito (ECU), 14-20.10.2024, 2024_CH-S.AM_0001_S_J_01
Date of Event: 14-20.10.2024
Date of Sample Collection: 18.10.2024
Prohibited Substance(s): Betamethasone
Bar Code No.: 1417988

I. Introduction
1. The Fédération Équestre Internationale (the FEI) alleges that Martín Andrade committed a
violation of Article 2.1 of the Equine Controlled Medication Rules – The Presence of a
Controlled Medication Substance and/or its Metabolites or Markers in a Horse’s Sample. The
FEI notified Mr Andrade of the alleged charge in his capacity as the Person Responsible.
2. Applicable Rules Provisions:
▪ Statutes 24th edition, effective 21 November 2023 (Statutes).
▪ General Regulations, 24th edition, updates effective 1 January 2024 (GRs).
▪ Internal Regulations of the FEI Tribunal, 4th Edition, 1 February 2025 (IRs).
▪ FEI’s Equine Anti-Doping and Controlled Medication Rules, 3rd Edition, updates
effective 1 January 2023 (EADCMRs).
▪ FEI’s 2024 Equine Prohibited Substances List (Equine Prohibited List)
3. All the words used in this Decision beginning with a capital letter and not previously
defined have the meaning set forth in the specific definitions of the Statutes, GRs, IRs, the
Equine Prohibited List and the EADCMRs. The Equine Controlled Medication Rules (the
ECM Rules) are set out in the EADCMRs.
II. Factual background
4. Martín Andrade de la Torre (FEI ID 10154649), is an Ecuadorian horse rider (the Person
Responsible or the PR), who competed as a junior rider in the FEI Jumping South
American Youth Championship in Quito, Ecuador, from 14 to 20 October 2024 (the
Event), with his horse, Topaze Z (the Horse). Mr Andrade was born on 28 June 2006, at
the time of the Event he was 18 years of age.
5. The FEI (together with the PR, the Parties), is the sole IOC recognised international
federation for equestrian sport. The FEI is the governing body of the FEI equestrian
disciplines of dressage, jumping, eventing, driving, endurance, vaulting, and para-
equestrian.
6. On 18 October 2024, blood and urine samples were collected from Topaze Z. The
samples were divided into an A and a B Sample and sent to a FEI Approved Laboratory
2

for analysis. The laboratory reported an Adverse Analytical Finding (the AAF) in the A
Sample for Betamethasone in the urine.
7. Betamethasone is a corticosteroid used in the treatment of dermatological, rheumatic
and allergic disease. It is a Controlled Medication Substance under the 2024 FEI Equine
Prohibited Substances List and is therefore prohibited in a horse's body during an Event
without a valid Veterinary Form under Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules.
8. The estimated concentration of Betamethasone in the A Sample was approximately 650
ng/ml. This estimate was derived by the Laboratory from a comparison of peak responses
against the spiked positive controls analysed alongside the A Sample.
9. It is not in dispute between the Parties that Topaze Z received intra-articular injections of
Betamethasone to the distal intertarsal joint (medial) and tarsometatarsal joint (lateral)
of both hocks on 30 September 2024, 18 days before the Sample was collected at the
Event. The injections were administered following a routine check in which a minor
lameness was identified in the Horse, and were performed by two of the PR's
veterinarians, both FEI-accredited.
III. Procedural background
10. On 18 November 2024, the FEI informed the PR of a possible violation of Article 2.1 of
the ECM Rules (the Alleged ECM Violation) and the further right to request the analysis of
the B Sample (the Notification Letter). The FEI offered the PR to have his case processed
under the Administrative Procedure, with the following proposed consequences:
10.1 Disqualification of the results (if applicable) obtained by the PR and the
Horse from the whole Event and forfeiture of all prizes and prize money
won at the Event;
10.2 A fine of CHF 1,500; and
10.3 Costs of CHF 1,000, or CHF 2,000 if a B Sample analysis was requested
and the administrative consequences were accepted after the B Sample
analysis.
11. The PR was further informed that if he declined or failed to accept the Administrative
Procedure, the case would be submitted to the FEI Tribunal for a final decision. The FEI
decided not to provisionally suspend the PR, given that only one Controlled Medication
Substance was detected in the sample.
3

12. On 22 November 2024, the PR requested the analysis of the B Sample.
13. On 18 December 2024, the FEI informed the PR that the analysis of the B Sample
confirmed the presence of Betamethasone, maintaining the alleged violation as specified
in the Notification Letter.
14. The PR submitted his Response to the Alleged ECM Violation to the FEI, including the
Horse's medical history and a veterinary locomotor examination report dated 30
September 2024. The PR declined to accept the Administrative Procedure, confirmed
that the Horse had been administered intra-articular injections of Betamethasone on 30
September 2024 under the supervision of two FEI-accredited veterinarians, and set out
his explanations for the positive finding, asserting that he bore No Fault or Negligence
for the violation.
15. On 30 January 2025, the Federación Ecuatoriana de Deportes Ecuestres (the ECU-NF) sent a
letter to the FEI expressing its commitment to the principles of clean sport, while raising
several concerns in connection with the present matter, including the alleged impact of
high-altitude conditions in Quito on the pharmacokinetics of Betamethasone, the
application of the strict liability principle and procedural concerns arising during the
sampling process.
16. On 26 June 2025, the FEI responded to the ECU-NF letter of 30 January 2025 providing
explanations on the regulatory matters raised by the ECU-NF, including the distinction
between screening limits and thresholds, the distinction between detection times and
withdrawal times, and the availability of Elective Testing - which the FEI strongly
recommended following intra-articular administration. The FEI acknowledged the ECU-
NF's concerns regarding the conduct of the sampling officials and indicated that it would
look into the matter. Lastly, the FEI granted the PR a final deadline until 3 July 2025 to
accept the Administrative Sanctions.
17. On 21 July 2025, the ECU-NF confirmed to the FEI that the PR preferred to have his case
decided by the FEI Tribunal, rather than resolved through the Administrative Procedure.
18. On 30 April 2026, the FEI submitted its response and the case file (the FEI’s Response) to
the Tribunal for adjudication.
19. On 25 May 2026, the Tribunal Chair appointed a Sole Panel Member – Mr Agustín Fattal
Jaef - to decide this case. The Parties were asked to provide any objections to the
constitution of the Hearing Panel by 28 May 2026. In addition, the PR was invited to
respond to the FEI’s allegations by submitting a statement of defence and any supporting
4

evidence by 15 June 2026. Finally, the Tribunal Chair informed the Parties of their right to
request a hearing by 17 June 2026, at the latest.
20. On 26 May 2026, the FEI communicated it had no objections to the constitution of the
Panel. The PR did not object to the constitution of the hearing panel.
21. On 15 June 2026, the PR submitted his statement of defence (the Statement of Defence),
explicitly waiving his right to a hearing.
22. On 16 June 2026, the FEI agreed with the PR that no hearing was necessary and that the
case could be decided on the Parties’ written submissions.
IV. The Parties’ Submissions:1
A. Submissions by the PR
23. The PR submitted his response to the Alleged ECM Violation and his Statement of
Defence on 15 June 2026. The PR’s position is summarised as follows:
23.1 As a preliminary matter, the PR submitted that these proceedings concern
strictly an alleged violation of Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules for the trace detection
of Betamethasone and not an Equine Anti-Doping violation for a Banned
Substance. The PR requested that all references to "Anti-Doping" be removed
from the FEI's submissions.
23.2 The PR submitted that he had always acted with transparency and good faith,
and with utmost caution, warranting a finding of No Fault or Negligence or, in
the alternative, No Significant Fault or Negligence.
23.3 The PR submitted that he had strictly adhered to the FEI Code of Conduct for
the Welfare of the Horse. In particular:
(a) the Horse’s fitness to compete was confirmed by routine check-ups,
(b) advice was obtained from two FEI-accredited veterinarians, Dr Sebastián
González and the supervision of Dr José Naranjo;
1 The following section is a summary of the relevant facts and evidence of the Parties’ written and oral submissions
and the written statements of the PR’s witnesses and expert.
5

(c) the treatment administered on 30 September 2024 consisted of a
therapeutic intra-articular injection of 24 mg of Betamethasone
(Betavet), a dose lower than the reference in the FEI List of Detection
Times (30 mg dose);
(d) the veterinary team consulted both the FEI List of Detection Times -
which publishes a seven-day (168 hour) baseline detection window - and
the Betavet product information - which states compliance with the ARCI,
RMTC, and USEF requirements for the shortest withdrawal time of 7
days; and
(e) a 14-day withdrawal period was observed before competition,
representing a 100% safety margin over the seven-day detection time
published by the FEI.
23.4 The PR further submitted that no Veterinary Form could have been filed because
the treatment was administered out of competition and did not fall within the
circumstances contemplated by Articles 1059 or 1061 of the FEI Veterinary
Regulations.
23.5 The PR argued that the detection of Betamethasone 18 days after
administration constituted an unpredictable biological anomaly. Relying in part
on the FEI’s own submissions, he argued that localised tissue leakage following
intra-articular administration can unpredictably extend the excretion period
beyond the published detection time.
23.6 The PR further contended that the scientific data underlying the screening limit
for Betamethasone is limited and that a reasonable athlete and veterinarian
could not have anticipated such an outcome.
23.7 In a youth athlete context, a rider who implemented a withdrawal period twice
the published detection time could not reasonably have been expected to
anticipate such a biological leakage anomaly.
23.8 The PR challenged the reliability of the analytical results on several grounds:
(a) Betamethasone is not included in Annex C of the FEI Standard for
Laboratories, which the PR submitted undermines the presumption that the
analysis was conducted in accordance with that standard;
6

(b) the FEI Standard for Laboratories does not account for the pharmacokinetic
effects of high-altitude conditions;
(c) the FEI Standards are outdated in relation to Betamethasone in light of
developments in the racing industry; and
(d) urine is not the most reliable matrix for assessing Betamethasone’s
pharmacological activity at the time of competition.
23.9 The PR further submitted that the FEI has failed to meet its burden of proof
under Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules, arguing that the FEI must establish not only
the presence of Betamethasone, but also its potential to affect performance or
horse welfare during competition.
23.10 The PR also relied on the absence of Xylazine in the Sample, submitting that,
because both substances were administered during the same veterinary
treatment, the negative Xylazine result supported his account that no
subsequent administration of Betamethasone occurred closer to the
competition.
23.11 In his first submission to the FEI, the PR raised concerns regarding the sample
collection process, alleging that the testing official acted in a rushed and
dismissive manner, prevented him from cooling down the Horse or contacting
his parents or trainer, and relied on a language barrier when appointing a
witness. The PR nevertheless clarified in his Statement of Defence that he did
not challenge the validity of the laboratory analysis.
23.12 The PR waived his right to an oral hearing, submitting that the matter could be
decided on the basis of the written exchanges.
23.13 With respect to the financial consequences, the PR relied on the following
circumstances:
(a) the PR is a non-professional student and Junior Category competitor with
zero equestrian income;
(b) this is a first offence for both the Horse and the rider;
(c) the trace detection results from a biological leakage anomaly accepted by
the FEI as the accurate source;
7

(d) at 18 years and three months of age, the PR narrowly missed the procedural
protections afforded to Minors under Appendix 1 of the EADCMRs;
(e) no administrative delays are attributable to the PR, who was cooperative
throughout and waived his right to a hearing; and
(f) in support of a zero-cost order, the PR relied on the FEI Tribunal decisions in
Jaafar Merza Hassan (Case 2023/FT55) and Fahad Helal Al Khatri (Case
2023/CM10).
23.14 The PR requested that the FEI Tribunal:
(i) confirm that he had established the source of the Controlled Medication
Substance;
(ii) find that he bore No Fault or Negligence under Article 10.5 of the ECM Rules
or, in the alternative, No Significant Fault or Negligence under Article 10.6.2;
(iii) backdates any sanction to 18 October 2024 pursuant to Article 10.12.2 of
the ECM Rules, on the basis that the 18-month administrative delay - during
which the PR voluntarily withdrew from representing Ecuador at the
Bolivarian Games;
(iv) impose no financial fine; and
(v) order no contribution towards legal costs.
B. Submissions by the FEI:
24. On 30 April 2026, the FEI submitted its Response to the Tribunal, which is summarised
as follows:
24.1 Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules is a strict liability offence. Accordingly, the presence
of a Controlled Medication Substance in a Horse’s Sample during an Event, in
the absence of a valid Veterinary Form, constitutes a violation regardless of
intent, fault, negligence, or knowing use.
24.2 The FEI submitted that both the A and B Sample analyses confirmed the
presence of Betamethasone in TOPAZE Z’s Sample and that, as no threshold
applies to Betamethasone, any concentration exceeding the applicable
8

screening limit constitutes an ECM Rule violation.
24.3 It further noted that no valid Veterinary Form had been submitted.
24.4 Relying on an expert opinion of Dr Caterina Termine, Senior Veterinary Advisor
at the FEI, the FEI submitted that:
(a) no departures from the FEI Standard for Laboratories occurred;
(b) the laboratory complied with all applicable standards;
(c) Annex C of the FEI Standard for Laboratories does not contain screening
limits applicable to EADCM samples; and
(d) the applicable screening limit for Betamethasone had been exceeded,
resulting in an Adverse Analytical Finding.
24.5 The FEI rejected the PR’s challenges to the violation, submitting that:
(a) the strict liability principle is not inconsistent with the FEI's rationale: fault is
relevant only to the consequences of the violation, not to its establishment.
(b) the FEI had discharged its burden of proof under Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules
by establishing the presence of Betamethasone, a Controlled Medication
Substance, in the Horse’s Sample;
(c) the PR did not established any departure from the FEI laboratory standards
capable of causing an Adverse Analytical Finding;
(d) it is for the PR and his Support Personnel to account for all factors affecting
medication elimination - including high altitude - and to adjust withdrawal
times accordingly, even beyond the FEI List of Detection Times. The FEI is not
aware of any studies examining Betamethasone pharmacokinetics at high
altitude;
(e) both urine and blood samples are reliable detection methods, either may
independently establish an Adverse Analytical Finding under Article 2.1.2 of
the ECM Rules;
(f) external regulatory frameworks, including racing and human anti-doping
regulations, are not applicable within the FEI regulatory system;
9

(g) the absence of Xylazine in the Sample was irrelevant to the presence of
Betamethasone.
24.6 As regards the source of the Controlled Medication Substance, the FEI accepted
that the PR had established, on a balance of probabilities, that the Betamethasone
detected originated from the intra-articular injections administered on 30
September 2024 for therapeutic purposes.
24.7 With respect to Fault, the FEI acknowledged several mitigating circumstances,
including that: (i) the treatment was administered out of competition for a
legitimate therapeutic purpose; (ii) it was performed by FEI-accredited
veterinarians; (iii) a withdrawal period of fourteen days, exceeding the published
detection time, was observed; (iv) the PR was 18 years old and relied on his
veterinarian’s advice.
24.8 Nevertheless, the FEI submitted that a finding of No Fault or Negligence was not
available under Article 10.4 of the ECM Rules, as the administration was carried out
by the PR’s veterinary personnel. The FEI maintained that PRs remain responsible
for the actions of their veterinary personnel and for ensuring compliance with the
applicable rules.
24.9 The FEI respectfully requested that the Panel issue a decision:
(i) upholding the charge that the PR has violated Article 2.1 of the EMC Rules;
(ii) imposing a period of Ineligibility of one (1) month on the PR in accordance
with Article 10.6.2 of the ECM Rules, commencing on the date to be decided
by
the FEI Tribunal in accordance with Article 10.12.2 of the ECM Rules;
(iii) disqualifying the results of the PR and Horse combination obtained at the
Event and the consequent forfeiture of all medals, points, prize money and
other
benefits won, pursuant to Articles 9 and 10.1.2 of the ECM Rules;
(iv) fining the PR in the amount of CHF 1,000;
(v) ordering the PR to pay the legal costs of 1’500 CHF that the FEI has incurred
in these proceedings; and
10

(vi) ordering the PR to pay the costs of the B Sample analysis in the amount of
1’000 CHF.
V. Legal Analysis
A. Jurisdiction
25. The Tribunal has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to Article 38 of the Statutes, Article
161 of the GRs, Article 8.1.1 of the ECM Rules and Article 18 of the IRs. The PR is a member
of the ECU-NF, which is a member of the FEI; therefore, the PR is bound by the ECM Rules.
B. Legal Discussion
26. Although the Panel has fully considered all the facts, legal arguments and evidence in the
present proceedings, it refers only to the facts and evidence it considers necessary to
explain its reasoning in this decision.
i. The ECM Rule Violation
27. Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules establishes that the FEI bears the burden of establishing an
ECM Rule violation on the balance of probabilities.
28. Article 3.2 of the ECM Rules establishes the methods by which facts may be established.
FEI-Approved Laboratories are presumed to have conducted Sample analysis and
custodial procedures in accordance with the FEI Standard for Laboratories. This
presumption may be rebutted by establishing, on a balance of probabilities, that a
departure from the FEI Standard for Laboratories occurred which could reasonably have
caused the Adverse Analytical Finding.
29. As per Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules, the presence of a Controlled Medication Substance in a
Horse's Sample — without a valid Veterinary Form — is sufficient proof of a violation. The
violation is one of strict liability: it is not necessary to establish intent, Fault, negligence or
knowing Use.
30. The Panel is satisfied that the analysis of the A and B samples confirmed the presence of
Betamethasone in the Horse’s system. The Panel notes that the PR does not dispute this
fact.
11

31. Betamethasone is a Controlled Medication Substance under the 2024 Equine Prohibited
Substances List. No quantitative threshold applies to Betamethasone and therefore any
quantity above the applicable screening limit constitutes an Adverse Analytical Finding.
Moreover, no valid veterinary form was submitted by the PR.
32. For these reasons, the Panel is satisfied that the FEI has established the ECM Rule violation
on a balance of probabilities in accordance with Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules.
ii. Elimination or Reduction of the Period of Ineligibility
33. Pursuant to Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules, a PR with no prior violations who commits an
Article 2.1 violation is subject to a presumptive period of Ineligibility of six (6) months,
subject to a potential elimination, reduction or suspension pursuant to Articles 10.5, 10.6
or 10.7 of the ECM Rules.
34. The presumptive period of Ineligibility may be eliminated pursuant to Article 10.5 of the
ECM Rules where the PR establishes both: (i) how the Prohibited Substance entered the
Horse's system; and (ii) that he bears No Fault or Negligence.
35. Separately, where the threshold requirement is met but No Fault or Negligence is not
established, the PR may nonetheless seek a reduction of the presumptive period of
ineligibility pursuant to Article 10.6 of the ECM Rules on the basis of No Significant Fault
or Negligence or on the basis of Article 10.7 of the ECM Rules for reasons other than
Fault.
1. Origin of the Substance
36. The PR submitted that the Betamethasone was administered to Topaze Z by means of
intra-articular injections to both hocks on 30 September 2024, performed by FEI-
accredited veterinarians.
37. This account was corroborated by the Horse's medical records (Exhibit 13.2) and the
veterinary locomotor examination report dated 30 September 2024 (Exhibit 13.3).
38. The FEI accepted, on a balance of probabilities, that the Betamethasone detected in
Topaze Z's Sample came most likely from the injections of 30 September 2024. The Panel
accepts the agreement between the Parties and therefore the threshold requirement is
satisfied.
12

2. No Fault or Negligence (Article 10.5 of the ECM Rules)
39. The Panel accordingly proceeds to assess the PR's degree of Fault or Negligence.
40. The PR sought a finding of No Fault or Negligence pursuant to Article 10.5 of the ECM
Rules. The Panel is mindful of the circumstances in which the PR finds himself: a young
rider who relied entirely on experienced, FEI-accredited veterinarians and who appears
to have acted in good faith throughout.
41. Nonetheless, Article 10.5 of the ECM Rules is unambiguous in providing that No Fault or
Negligence does not apply where the Controlled Medication Substance entered the
Horse's system through administration by the PR's veterinary personnel, even without
disclosure to the PR.
42. It is not disputed that the Betamethasone was administered by the PR's own
veterinarians.
43. The PR's responsibility is not extinguished by his delegation of veterinary decisions.
Consequently, the Panel finds that the No Fault or Negligence provision cannot be
applied.
3. No Significant Fault or Negligence (Article 10.6 of the ECM Rules)
44. The Panel turns now to analyse whether the PR has established No Significant Fault or
Negligence pursuant to Article 10.6 of the ECM Rules. The standard requires the PR to
demonstrate that his Fault or Negligence, when viewed in the totality of the
circumstances and with reference to the criteria for No Fault or Negligence, was not
significant in relation to the ECM Rule violation.
45. In conducting this assessment, the Panel has regard to the definition of Fault in Appendix
1 of the EADCMRs2, which directs it to consider, inter alia, the PR's experience and the
2 “Fault is any breach of duty or any lack of care appropriate to a particular situation. Factors to be taken into consideration
in assessing an Person Responsible and/or member of the Support Personnel’s and/or other Person’s degree of Fault
include, for example, the Person Responsible’s and/or member of the Support Personnel’s and/or other Person’s experience,
whether the Person Responsible and/or member of the Support Personnel and/or other Person is a Minor, special
considerations such as impairment, the degree of risk that should have been perceived by the Person Responsible and/or
member of the Support Personnel and/or other Person and the level of care and investigation exercised by the Person
Responsible and/or member of the Support Personnel and/or other Person in relation to what should have been the
perceived level of risk. In assessing the Person Responsible’s and/or member of the Support Personnel’s and/or other
Person’s degree of Fault, the circumstances considered must be specific and relevant to explain the Person Responsible’s
and/or member of the Support Personnel’s and/or other Person’s departure from the expected standard of behaviour. Thus,
for example, the fact that the Person Responsible would lose the opportunity to earn large sums of money during a period
of Ineligibility, or the fact that the Person Responsible only has a short time left in their career, or the timing of the sporting
calendar, would not be relevant factors to be considered in reducing the period of Ineligibility under Articles 10.6.1.”
13

level of care and investigation exercised relative to the perceived level of risk. The Panel
examines each relevant circumstance:
45.1 It is uncontested that the Betamethasone injections were performed Out-Of-
Competition to treat a minor lameness identified during a routine check. This is a
medically legitimate purpose. There is no suggestion, and the Panel finds no basis
to infer, that the treatment was administered with any intent to mask a condition
or enhance performance. The Panel accepts this as a mitigating circumstance and
gives it appropriate weight.
45.2 The injections were administered by the PR's long-standing and FEI-accredited
veterinarians. While the ECM Rules do not permit reliance on veterinary personnel
as a basis for eliminating personal responsibility, the Panel considers that the
identity and qualification of the treating veterinarians can be relevant to the
assessment of the PR's Fault. A PR who entrusts veterinary decisions to FEI-
accredited professionals exercises a meaningful degree of care. Therefore, the
Panel accepts this as a mitigating circumstance.
45.3 The PR's veterinary team cross-referenced the FEI List of Detection Times, which
publishes a seven-day (168-hour) baseline detection window for intra-articular
injections of Betamethasone at the administered dose. They then applied a 14-
day withdrawal buffer — i.e., double the published figure — before presenting the
beginning of the Competition.
The FEI List of Detection Times is explicitly described as a guide only, accompanied
by disclaimers to the effect that individual pharmacokinetic factors may affect
clearance times and that the published timelines cannot guarantee a negative
finding. Reliance on said guide may constitute a mitigating factor. This is in line
with the FEI’s own stance in other cases in which the Tribunal was requested to
accept the terms of settlement agreements. In such cases, the FEI accepted that
checking the withdrawal and detection times, and calculating a sufficient margin
constituted a mitigating factor.3
Having said that, in the Panel’s view, reliance on the FEI List of Detection Times
alone cannot constitute a mitigating factor of determinative weight. Instead, in
order to have an impact on the otherwise applicable sanction, such element must
be coupled with other attenuating elements, as is the case here.
3 C24-0046 (2024-FT38 WIEJANDIE QUALITO), par. 16 ff., C25-0014 (2024-CM10 MANSINI LTD) par. 21 ff.
14

45.4 The PR was 18 years and three months of age at the time of the ECM Rule
violation, competing in the Junior category at a regional youth championship. The
specific provisions for Minors in the ECM Rules therefore do not apply to him.
Nonetheless, his experience as a junior competitor are expressly contemplated
as relevant factor in the Fault definition in Appendix 1 of the EADCMRs and are
therefore accepted as an attenuating element.
46. The Panel has weighed these circumstances against the fact that the sampling occurred
18 days post-administration - well beyond the published detection window - and that no
Elective Testing was conducted prior to competition to confirm clearance.
47. The Panel notes that the FEI Veterinary Regulations provide for Elective Testing precisely
for situations where doubt can exist about the adequacy of a withdrawal period. The PR,
together with his veterinary team could reasonably have been expected to consider this
option, particularly given the acknowledged risk of tissue leakage from intra-articular
injections. This is a factor that weighs against the PR.
48. For all these reasons, the Panel finds that the PR has established, on a balance of
probabilities, that his Fault or Negligence, viewed in the totality of the circumstances, was
not significant in relation to the ECM Rule violation.
49. The Panel therefore finds that the PR is entitled to a reduction of the presumptive six-
month period of Ineligibility pursuant to Article 10.6.2 of the ECM Rules.
iii. Sanctions
50. Having found that the PR incurred in No Significant Fault or Negligence, the Panel must
determine the appropriate period of Ineligibility.
51. Pursuant to Article 10.6.2 of the ECM Rules, the Panel has discretion to reduce the period
of Ineligibility in light of the circumstances of the case. The FEI proposed a period of one
(1) month. Having regard to the mitigating factors set out above, the Panel considers this
to be an appropriate and proportionate sanction in the circumstances of this case.
52. Pursuant to Article 10.12.2 of the ECM Rules, the Panel may, in its discretion, order the
period of Ineligibility to commence at an earlier date, commencing as early as the date of
Sample collection.
53. In the present case, the sample was collected on 18 October 2024. The FEI presented
the case to the Tribunal on 30 April 2026, that is, more than 18 months after sample
collection.
15

54. It is not in dispute, and the FEI expressly acknowledged in its Response, that the delays
in the prosecution of this matter were not attributable to the PR. The PR provided his
explanations promptly, engaged constructively throughout the proceedings, and waived
his right to an oral hearing in the interest of procedural economy.
55. To impose the period of Ineligibility prospectively in these circumstances would expose
the PR to the consequences of delays entirely beyond his control - a result the Panel
considers inequitable and inconsistent with the purpose of Article 10.12.2.
56. The Panel accordingly orders that the one-month period of Ineligibility commences on
the date of sample collection, i.e., 18 October 2024.
57. Pursuant to Articles 9 and 10.1.2 of the ECM Rules, the results obtained by the PR and
Horse combination at the Event are automatically disqualified, with forfeiture of all
related medals, points, and prize money. The Panel notes that this consequence applies
regardless of the reduction or elimination of the period of Ineligibility under Article 10 of
the ECM Rules.
58. The FEI requested a fine of CHF 1,000. The Panel notes that Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules
provides for a fine of up to CHF 15,000 for a violation of Article 2.1. The FEI's request falls
at the lower end of this range and within the indicative amounts contained in the FEI
Guidelines for fines and contributions towards legal costs.4 Accordingly, the Panel
considers appropriate to impose a fine of one thousand Swiss francs (CHF 1,000) to the
PR.
59. Further, the FEI sought a contribution towards its legal costs of CHF 1,500. The Panel
notes that the FEI fulfilled its obligations in these proceedings - submitting a thorough
Response, adducing expert evidence from Dr Caterina Termine, and substantiating its
position on all relevant issues. Accordingly, the Panel grants the FEI's request and orders
the PR to pay a contribution towards the FEI's legal costs in the amount of one thousand
five hundred Swiss francs (CHF 1,500).
60. Finally, the PR is ordered to pay the costs of the B Sample analysis in the amount of 1’000
CHF.
4 According to these guidelines, a first ECM Rule violation with a reduction of the period of Ineligibility due to No
Significant Fault/Negligence may lead to a fine ranging between CHF 1,000 and CHF 3,000.
16

VI. Terms of the Decision
61. As a result, the Panel makes the following decision and imposes the following sanctions
in accordance with Article 164.11 of the GRs and Article 10 of the ECM Rules:
a) Mr Martín Andrade violated Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules.
b) Mr Martín Andrade is subject to a period of Ineligibility of one (1) month. The period
of Ineligibility commenced on 18 October 2024, the date of sample collection.
c) The results of the combination Mr Martín Andrade and Topaze Z at the Event are
disqualified, including the forfeiture of any prize money, medals and ranking points.
d) Mr Martín Andrade is ordered to pay a fine of one thousand Swiss francs (CHF 1,000).
e) Mr Martín Andrade is ordered to pay a contribution towards the FEI's legal costs in
the amount of one thousand five hundred Swiss francs (CHF 1,500).
f) Mr Martín Andrade is ordered to pay one thousand Swiss francs (1’000 CHF) to the
FEI for the cost of analysing the B sample.
62. Mr Martín Andrade, the ECU-NF, and the FEI will be notified of this Decision.
63. According to Article 170 of the GRs, this Tribunal Decision is effective from the day of
written notification to the persons and bodies concerned.
FOR THE TRIBUNAL
________________________________________
Mr Agustín Fattal Jaef, Sole Panel Member

In accordance with Article 12.3 of the ECM Rules the Parties may appeal this decision before
the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) within twenty-one (21) days of the present notification.

title: Final Decision Settlement Agreement C26-0006 Case 2025BS09 P G WITHERNAY Ms Lucy ROBINSON
text:
DECISION RENDERED BY THE FEI TRIBUNAL
9 July 2026
In the matter of
FÉDÉRATION EQUESTRE INTERNATIONALE (the “FEI”)
vs.
Ms. Lucy ROBINSON –Person Responsible (the “PR”)
together the “Parties”
(Reference No. FEI Tribunal: C26-0006 ROBINSON)
COMPOSITION OF THE FEI TRIBUNAL PANEL:
Ms. Diane Pitts, (USA), Sole Panel Member
FEI Case number: 2025/BS09 P G WITHERNAY - Ms. Lucy ROBINSON (GBR)
Horse/Passport: P G WITHERNAY/106NI31/GBR
Person Responsible/ID/NF: Lucy ROBINSON/10107550/GBR
Event/Date: CCI3*-L - Hartpury (GBR), 05 – 10.08.2025
Event/ID: 2025_CI_0671_C_S_02
Date of sample collection: 09.08.2025
Prohibited Substance(s): Trazodone
Bar Code No.: 1608754
1

All the words used in this Decision beginning with a capital letter and not otherwise defined
herein shall have the meaning set forth in the specific definitions of the FEI General
Regulations (the “GRs”) and Statutes (the” Statutes”), the FEI Veterinary Regulations (the
“VRs”), the 2025 Equine Prohibited Substance List and the Equine Anti-Doping and
Controlled Medication Regulations (the “EADCMRs”). The Equine Anti-Doping Rules (the
“EADRs” or “EAD Rules”) and the Equine Controlled Medication Rules (the “ECMRs” or “ECM
Rules”) are set out in the EADCMRs.
I. Introduction
1. This Decision pertains to the FEI case 2025/BS09 2025/BS09 P G WITHERNAY. In this
matter, the FEI notified the PR of a violation of Article 2.1 (The Presence of a Banned
Substance and/or its Metabolites or Markers in a Horse’s Sample) of the EAD Rules. This
violation was based on the positive finding of Trazodone in the Sample of the Horse
P G WITHERNAY (the “Horse”) which was collected at the CCI3*-L - Hartpury (GBR),
05 – 10.08.2025 (the “Event”).
2. The FEI and the PR agreed to a Settlement Agreement on 23 March 2026 (the
“Settlement Agreement”). The Settlement Agreement together with the attached
Exhibits are hereby incorporated by reference in this Decision.
II. Applicable Rule Provisions
3. The following regulations are applicable to the present case:
Statutes 25th edition, effective 21 November 2023.
General Regulations, 24thedition, 1 January 2020, updates effective 1 January 2025.
Internal Regulations of the FEI Tribunal, 4th Edition, 1 February 2025 (the “IRs”).
FEI Equine Anti-Doping and Controlled Medication Regulations, 4th edition, effective
1 January 2025.
FEI Veterinary Regulations, 15th edition 2023, effective 1 January 2025.
III. Factual background and initial proceedings
2

4. Ms Lucy ROBINSON (FEI ID 10107550) is a rider in the discipline of Eventing1 and
the PR in accordance with Article 118.3 of the GRs. She competed with the Horse at
the Event. The PR is a member of the British Equestrian Federation (the “GBR-NF”),
the latter being a member of the FEI. The PR is therefore bound by the EADRs.
5. The FEI is the sole IOC-recognised international governing body for the equestrian
sport disciplines of Dressage and Para-Dressage, Jumping, Eventing, Driving and
Para-Driving, Endurance and Vaulting.
6. At the Event, on 9 August 2025, during the cross-country phase, the PR submitted
that the Horse suffered a serious fall. She explained that the Horse was treated on
course with pain relief and sedation and was transported by horse ambulance to
the onsite equine hospital for further investigation. It was also submitted that at
approximately 17:15 on the same day, the PR was informed that the injuries to the
Horse were so severe that the only humane option was euthanasia and as such the
Horse was euthanised.
7. Due to the fatality of the Horse at this Event, the Horse was further tested on 9
August 2025. Blood samples (Sample no 1608754) were collected from the Horse
and sent to the FEI approved Laboratory, LGC Newmarket Road, Fordham,
Cambridgeshire (GBR) (the “Laboratory”), for analysis. The analysis of the blood
sample revealed the presence of Trazodone; an antidepressant used in the
treatment of depression and anxiety in humans. is classified as a Banned
Substance, which is prohibited at all times, under the FEI Equine Prohibited
Substances List.2
8. The positive finding of Trazodone in the Sample therefore gave rise to a violation of
the EAD Rules (the “EAD Rule Violation”).
9. The FEI informed the PR of the EAD Rule Violation in a notification letter dated 23
September 2025 (the “Notification Letter”). In accordance with Article 7.4.1. of the
EAD Rules, the FEI provisionally suspended the PR as of the date of the Notification
Letter (the “Provisional Suspension”).
1 Please note it originally stated in the Settlement Agreement that Ms. Lucy ROBINSON (FEI ID: 10107550), the Person
Responsible (“PR”) in accordance with Article 118.3 of the FEI General Regulations, is a show jumping rider competing for Great
Britain however she is a PR in the discipline of Eventing.
2 2025 FEI Equine Prohibited Substances List.
https://inside.fei.org/sites/default/files/2025%20Prohibited%20Substances%20List.pdf
3

10. The PR had the right to request an analysis of the B Sample. The Owner of the Horse
requested the B Sample analysis on 29 September 2025.The B Sample analysis of
the blood sample confirmed the presence of Trazodone. The PR was notified of the
results of the B Sample testing by letter dated 27 October 2025.
11. In the Notification Letter, the FEI further informed the PR of her right to provide an
explanation within 20 days from the date of the Notification Letter.
12. The PR submitted her written explanations on 24 November 2025, supplemented
by additional evidence on 26 and 28 January 2026, which were as follows:
a. The Horse was prescribed Sucralfate powder by a veterinarian to be
administered in the morning feed in order to treat the Horse’s gastric ulcers;
b. In June 2025, the PR visited the Owners of the Horse (together with the Horse)
as she was offered to have a training session with the previous trainer of this
Horse (who is also a family friend of the Owners). The PR stayed on their farm
one night and she took with her the prescribed medication, Sucralfate as well
as the Horse’s feed, hay and all other equipment;
c. The PR left the Owners farm on 27 June 2025 where she forgot and left
behind the Horse’s medication Sucralfate. The PR was not worried about it as
she had another tub of this medication at home;
d. The Sucralfate container was returned by the Owners to the PR on 27 July
2025 i.e., one month later, and as of that day the PR started to use the
medication from the returned container;
e. The Horse underwent the doping control sampling at the Event on 9 August
2025;
f. Following the notice of the Rule violation, it was discovered that a person that
helped the Owners with their other horses (the “Helper”), contaminated the
Sucralfate medication with Trazodone while it was left at the Owner’s farm
(and when the PR had already left). Another horse of the Owner, BELINDA,
was prescribed Trazodone by a veterinarian; when preparing the meal for
BELINDA, the Helper measured a dose of Trazodone but as it was not enough,
the Helper topped it up with the Sucralfate medication that was stored in the
medical cabinet (assuming that it was the same medication as Trazodone as
the containers looked the same). The Helper then put the spoon that she
used (from Trazodone medication) in the container of Sucralfate;
g. The PR submitted expert opinion of Dr Emmanuel Strahm stating that “the
measured level of trazodone contamination in the Sucralfate is fully consistent
with the blood concentration detected in the Horse. Dr. Strahm concludes that the
contamination scenario is highly probable and adequately accounts for the
laboratory findings.” ;
4

h. The PR provided additional supporting evidence and documents in order to
corroborate her explanations, namely:
- Medical records of the Horse P G WITHERNAY, confirming the medical
condition of gastric ulcers and the prescribed treatment with the
medication Sucralfate;
- Medical records of the other leisure Horse Belinda and the prescribed
medication Trazodone;
- Lab analysis of the unopened medication of Sucralfate (which tested
negative to Trazodone);
- Lab analysis of the Sucralfate medication used by the PR (which tested
positive to Trazodone);
- Lab analysis of various products and supplements used by the PR – all of
those products tested negative to Trazodone;
- Dr Strahm Opinion Letter confirming the scientific plausibility of the
provided explanations by the PR;
- Testimonies of the PR, the Owner and the trainer which all confirm the
occurrence of the above-mentioned events;
- Testimony of the Helper who mixed up the two medications;
- Pictures of the packages of the two medications, the spoon and the
powders themselves (which appear easy to mix up if one does not read
the label).
i. Consequently, Trazodone detected in the Horse’s Sample, more likely than
not came from the medication Sucralfate that was inadvertently
contaminated by the Helper when preparing the meal for the Horse BELINDA.
This came to the PR’s and Owner’s attention only after the PR received the FEI
Notification Letter of 23 September 2025. As such, the PR bears No Fault or
Negligence (or, in the alternative, No Significant Fault or Negligence) for the
presence of Trazodone in the Horse’s sample.
13. In order to verify the provided explanations, the FEI consulted its external scientific
expert as to whether those explanations, as compared to the concentration of
Trazodone detected in the Horse’s Sample, are scientifically plausible and whether
the provided explanations could indeed be the source of the positive finding. The
FEI expert confirmed that those explanations are indeed scientifically plausible.
14. The FEI therefore agreed that the PR’s explanation of the source was consistent with
the Adverse Analytical Finding in the Horse, and was therefore satisfied that the PR
has established, on a balance of probabilities, how Trazodone entered the Horse’s
system.
5

15. Fault and Negligence for the rule violation- In evaluating the PR’s level of fault or
negligence, if any, for the Rule Violation under Art. 2.1 of the EADRs, the FEI took
into account in particular the following considerations:
- Neither the PR, nor the Owner of the Horse were aware of the
contamination of the Sucralfate medication by the Helper before they
received the FEI Notification Letter dated 23 September 2025. The PR used
the returned Sucralfate medication in good faith and did not suspect at
any point that it could have been contaminated with a Prohibited
Substance by a third person as there were no obvious external signs that
the Sucralfate has been tampered with;
- The PR was well aware of her antidoping obligations and her general
approach to horse management shows a high standard of care, both, at
home stables and at competitions;
- On the other hand, the FEI noted that under anti-doping jurisprudence,
the CAS strictly maintains that athletes who fail to secure their medications
– leaving it without supervision or not “under lock” – cannot establish a
plea of No Fault or Negligence as they did not exercise the “utmost
caution”.;
- In the case of CAS 2005/A/951, Canas v. ATP, the CAS Panel held that “a
player is being clearly negligent when relying blindly on the system set up to
take care of him at a Tournament site, assuming that it is foolproof. The player
has a duty of utmost caution after visiting the Tournament doctor, when
actually ingesting medications. It would be normal for him to rely on the
trustworthiness and knowledge of the Tournament doctor if the doctor handed
the medications to him, but any professional athlete these days has to be wary
when, as in this case, he receives medications which, he knows, have gone
through several hands. Thus, the player cannot establish that he bears No Fault
or Negligence for the Doping Offense. What is determinative of the level of fault
or negligence is not only what the player actually knew or expected but also
what he could have suspected.”3;
- The above-mentioned principle was further confirmed in the case CAS
2011/A/2512 (WADA v. FIS & Kontinen) and the case CAS 2006/A/1025
Mariano Puerta v. International Tennis Federation (ITF), both of which did
echo and rely on the same principle that an athlete must exercise “utmost
caution” with respect to substances ingested and that loss of control, lack
of safeguards, or unattended exposure undermines any claim of “No Fault
or Negligence” (confirming at the same time that athletes can benefit in
those cases from No Significant Fault or Negligence provision);
3 CAS 2005/A/951, Canas v. ATP, page 1, available at: https://jurisprudence.tas-cas.org/pdf/951.pdf
6

- The FEI furthermore noted that although Trazodone was listed as a
Banned Substance under the 2025 FEI Prohibited Substance List, there
were changes made to the 2026 FEI Prohibited Substance List4 and
Trazodone is classified currently as a Controlled Medication;
- According to article 24.2.2 “Any EAD Rule violation case which is pending as
of the Effective Date and any EAD Rule violation case brought after the Effective
Date based on an EAD Rule violation which occurred prior to the Effective Date,
shall be governed by the substantive EAD Rule in effect at the time the alleged
EAD Rule violation occurred, and not by the substantive EAD Rule set out in
these EAD Rules, unless the panel hearing the case determines the principle of
“lex mitior” appropriately applies under the circumstances of the case.”;
- As Trazodone cases are currently prosecuted under the Controlled
Medication Rules for which the maximum sanction is 6 months of
ineligibility (or even an Administrative Procedure, if it is a first violation for
the PR and the Horse), the FEI submits that indeed lex mitior is applicable
to the current proceedings and the fairness requires that the ineligibility
period applicable to the current matter be assessed accordingly;
- Given the overall circumstances of the case at hand, the FEI agreed that
the PR bore No Significant Fault or Negligence for her EADCMR rule
violation and her level of Fault/Negligence falls in the lower range of the
applicable sanction.
16. For the reasons stated above, the FEI concluded that the PR established that she
bore No Significant Fault or Negligence for the EAD rule violation and the period of
ineligibly should therefore be reduced in accordance with the Article 10.6.1.2
EADCMR and lex mitior principle and shall amount to two (2) months ineligibility
period.
17. In accordance with the Articles 9.1 and 10.1.2 of the EADR, the FEI confirmed that
results achieved by the PR and the Horse at the Event are disqualified, with all
resulting consequences, including forfeiture of any related medals, points and
prizes, regardless of the level of fault.
18. The FEI also noted that lex mitior principle should be applied to the fine imposed on
the PR and should therefore amount to 1’500 CHF in accordance with the FEI
Guidelines for Fines and Contributions Towards Legal Costs5 applicable to the
4 2026 FEI Equine Prohibited Substances List.
https://inside.fei.org/sites/default/files/2026%20Prohibited%20Substances%20List.pdf
5 FEI Guidelines for Fines and Contributions towards Legal Costs, effective as of 1 January 2025, available at:
https://inside.fei.org/sites/default/files/FEI_Guidelines_Legal_Costs%20-%20Final%20-
%20Effective%20as%20of%201%20January%202025.pdf
7

Controlled Medication violations. Finally, as the case was concluded with a
Settlement Agreement the FEI does not seek any contribution to the legal costs.
19. On 23 March 2026 January 2026, the FEI notified the Tribunal that it had reached a
settlement of the dispute with the PR, which included the reduction of the period of
Ineligibility to be imposed on the PR.
20. On 1 April 2026, the Tribunal informed the Parties of the appointment of a one-
person hearing panel (the “Hearing Panel”) to adjudicate and approve this case. The
Parties were asked to provide any objections to the constitution of the Hearing
Panel by 6 April 2026.
21. On 2 April 2026, the FEI confirmed having no objection to the constitution of the
Hearing Panel.
22. The PR did not submit any objection to the constitution of the Hearing Panel.
IV. Accepted Terms
23. The Settlement Agreement is made in accordance with Article 10.8.2 of the EAD
Rules and is subject to the approval of the Tribunal. Article 10.8.2 of the EADR
permits for an agreement between the parties, subject to the FEI Tribunal’s
approval.
24. In the matter of the Adverse Analytical Finding related to the samples, which were
collected from the PR’s Horse P G WITHERNAY in the CCI3*-L - Hartpury (GBR), held
between 5 and 10 August 2025, the PR and the FEI agree in accordance with the
Article 10.8.2 of the EADR on the following:
a) The PR admits the violation of Article 2.1 EADR (The presence of a Banned
Substance and/or its Metabolites or Markers in a Horse’s Sample);
b) The PR established on a balance of probabilities how Trazodone entered the
Horse’s system;
c) The PR established that she bore No Significant Fault or Negligence for the
rule violation in accordance with Article 10.6.1.2 EADCMR and the period of
Ineligibility imposed on the PR shall amount to two (2) months of
suspension, commencing as of the date of the final FEI Tribunal Decision
(the Provisional Suspension served by the PR shall be credited against the
imposed period of Ineligibility);
8

d) The results achieved by the PR and the Horse at the Event are disqualified,
with all resulting consequences, including forfeiture of any related medals,
points and prizes, in accordance with Articles 9.1 and 10.1.2 of the EADRs;
e) The PR shall pay a fine of 1’500 CHF;
f) Each party will bear its own legal and other costs incurred in connection
with these proceedings;
g) No other Sanctions will apply in this case;
h) This violation of the EADCMRs shall be considered a prior violation for the
purpose of Multiple Violations in accordance with Article 10.9 of the
EADCMRs.
25. This agreement is made in accordance with Article 10.8.2 of the EADR and is subject
to the approval of the FEI Tribunal. The Parties hereby kindly request that the FEI
Tribunal issue a Decision incorporating the terms of this agreement.
26. In accordance with the Article 10.8.2 of the EADR, the Decision by the FEI to enter
or not enter into a case resolution agreement, and the amount of the reduction to,
and the starting date of, the period of Ineligibility and the confirmation of the case
resolution agreement by the FEI Tribunal are not subject to appeal under Article 13
of the EADR.
27. The parties acknowledge and agree that pursuant to Article 14.3 of the EADR, the
Decision will be made public by the FEI.
28. The terms set out in the agreement have been agreed as a full and final settlement
of all claims relating to the subject-matter of these proceedings. Accordingly, any
and all other claims for relief that any party might otherwise have made against
another in relation to the subject-matter of these proceedings are released and
discharged unconditionally, and they may not be pursued in any form hereafter.
V. Decision
29. The Tribunal has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to Article 38 of the Statutes,
Article 159 of the GRs, the EADCMR Rules, the VRs and Article 18 of the IRs. The PR
is a member of the GBR-NF, which is a member of the FEI. The PR is therefore bound
by the EADRs.
30. Having reviewed the case summary, the full reasoning of the Settlement Agreement
9

and the Accepted Terms, the Hearing Panel takes note that the FEI has agreed that
the PR established, on a balance of probabilities, how Trazodone entered the
Horse’s system.
31. The Hearing Panel further acknowledges that the PR and the FEI have agreed on
the terms to conclude these proceedings, in accordance with Article 10.8.2 of the
EAD Rules, as detailed under Section IV of this Final Decision.
32. The Hearing Panel confirms that the Accepted Terms of the Settlement Agreement
comply with the EAD Rules and finds no grounds to object to them.
33. In particular, the Hearing Panel notes that, in view of the Settlement Agreement
reached by the parties that the PR bears No Significant Fault or Negligence for the
EAD Rule Violation, the period of Ineligibility imposed on the PR is reduced to a
period of two months, starting as at the date of the Provisional Suspension.
34. Therefore, and in accordance with the mutual consent of the Parties, the Hearing
Panel hereby directs the Parties to fully comply with all the terms of the Settlement
Agreement. Furthermore, this Final Decision concludes this case, C26-0006
ROBINSON, 2025/BS09 P G WITHERNAY
35. The Parties acknowledge and agree that pursuant to Article 13.3 of the EAD Rules,
this Final Decision will be made public by the FEI. The terms set out in the Settlement
Agreement are full and final settlement of all claims relating to the subject matter
of these proceedings.
36. The Settlement Agreement and this Final Decision are not subject to appeal under
Article 12 of the EAD Rules.
DECISION TO BE FORWARDED TO:
a. The Parties: Yes
b. The Secretary General of the NF of the person sanctioned: Yes
c. Any other: No
FOR THE FEI TRIBUNAL
______________________________________________________________________
Ms Diane Pitts, One-Member Panel

title: FEI Tribunal Final Decision C25-0040 Case 2025FT21 DENALI QH - Mr F WALEED (APR)
text:
DECISION of the FEI TRIBUNAL
28 April 2026
In the matter of
Mr. Fahad WALEED - Additional Person Responsible (Trainer) - (PR: Ref. C25-0040)
(FEI Case number: 2025/FT21 DENALI QH)
FEI Tribunal Hearing Panel: Ms Diane Pitts (USA)
FEI Tribunal Reference: C25-0040 [FEI 2025/FT21 DENALI QH]
Person Responsible/ID/NF: Majed ALQAHTANI/10363591/KSA
Trainer/ID/NF: Fahad WALEED/10306368/KSA
Event/Date: CEI1* 100 - Riyadh (KSA), 24-26.04.2025
Event/Code: 2025_CI_0266_E_S_02
Date of sample collection: 26.04.2025
Prohibited Substance(s): Triamcinolone Acetonide
Bar Code Nos.: 1417731

I. Introduction
1. The Fédération Équestre Internationale (the FEI) alleges that Mr Fahad WALEED
committed a violation of Article 2.1 of the Equine Anti-Doping & Controlled Medication
Rules – The Presence of a Controlled Medication Substance and/or its Metabolites or Markers
in a Horse’s Sample. The FEI notified Mr. WALEED of the alleged charge in his capacity as
the Trainer and Additional Person Responsible (the APR).
2. Applicable Rules Provisions:
▪ Statutes 25th edition, effective 21 November 2023 (Statutes).
▪ General Regulations, 24th edition, updates effective 1 January 2025 (GRs).
▪ Internal Regulations of the FEI Tribunal, 4th Edition, 1 February 2025 (IRs).
▪ FEI’s Equine Anti-Doping and Controlled Medication Rules, 4th Edition, updates
effective 1 January 2025 (EADCMRs).
▪ FEI’s 2025 Equine Prohibited Substances List (Equine Prohibited List)
3. All the words used in this Decision beginning with a capital letter and not otherwise
defined have the meaning set forth in the specific definitions of the Statutes, GRs, IRs, the
Equine Prohibited List and the EADCMRs. The Equine Anti-Doping Rules (the EAD Rules)
and the Equine Controlled Medication Rules (the ECM Rules) are set out in the EADCMRs.
II. Factual background
4. The APR is a registered Trainer from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (the KSA-NF) and was the
registered trainer for the horse DENALI QH (the Horse), FEI ID 109AP47, which competed
with its rider Mr. Majed ALQAHTANI (the Person Responsible or the PR) FEI ID: 10363591, at
the CEI1* 100 in Riyadh (KSA), on 24-26.04.25 (the Event).
5. The FEI (together with the APR, the Parties), is the sole IOC-recognised international
federation for equestrian sport. The FEI is the governing body of the FEI equestrian
disciplines of dressage and para-dressage, jumping, eventing, driving and para-driving,
endurance, and vaulting.
2

6. Blood samples were collected from the Horse on 26 April 2025 at the Event. The Horse’s
sample returned a positive finding for Triamcinolone Acetonide, a Prohibited Substance
under the Equine Prohibited List.
7. Triamcinolone Acetonide is a corticosteroid anti-inflammatory agent used in the
treatment of orthopaedic disease. It is classified as a Controlled Medication Substance
under the Equine Prohibited List.
III. Procedural background
8. On 19 May 2025, the FEI informed the APR of a possible violation of Article 2.1 of the ECM
Rules (the Notification Letter).
9. In the Notification Letter, the APR was informed that he had the right to request the
Horse’s B sample to be analysed. The B-Sample analysis was not requested.
10. Despite various attempt by the FEI to correspond with the APR, no reply by the APR was
ever received despite numerous reminders i.e., 24 June 2025 and 25 August 2025
wherein FEI sent emails to the APR and the KSA-NF.
11. In accordance with Article 8.3.6 of the ECM Rules, if the Person Responsible and/or
member of the Support Personnel (where applicable) does not elect the Administrative
Procedure within the fixed time limit, the Administrative Sanctions shall be considered
declined, and the case shall be submitted to the FEI Tribunal (the Tribunal) for final
Decision.
12. On 15 December 2025, the FEI submitted its response and the case file (the FEI’s
Response) to the Tribunal for adjudication.
13. On 19 December 2025, the Tribunal Chair appointed a one-person Hearing Panel (the
Panel) to decide this case. The Parties were asked to provide any objections to the
constitution of the Panel by 7 January 2026. In addition, the APR was invited to respond
to the FEI’s allegations by submitting a statement of defence and any supporting evidence
by 26 January 2026. Finally, the Tribunal Chair informed the Parties of their right to
request a hearing by 29 January 2026, at the latest.
14. On 19 December 2025, the FEI confirmed having no objection to the constitution of the
Panel. The APR never replied; therefore, his silence was taken as agreement to the
constitution of the Panel.
3

15. The APR did not file a formal submission or request a hearing despite having been
notified of the Tribunal’s letter via email directly to him and through the KSA-NF.
Therefore, the Final Decision was rendered by the Sole Panel Member based on the
papers submitted within the deadline.
IV. The Parties’ Submissions:1
A. Submissions by the APR
16. The APR made no submissions.
B. Submissions by the FEI:
17. On 15 December 2025, the FEI submitted the FEI Response to the Tribunal. The FEI’s
position is summarised as follows:
▪ Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules makes it the FEI’s burden to establish all of the
elements of the ECM Rule violation to the comfortable satisfaction of the FEI
Tribunal;
▪ The elements of an Article 2.1 violation are straightforward. 'It is not necessary that
intent, fault, negligence or knowing Use be demonstrated in order to establish an ECM
Rule violation under Article 2.1'. Instead, it is a 'strict liability' offence, established
simply by proof that a Prohibited Substance(s) was present in the Horse's Sample;
▪ The result of the analysis of the A Sample taken from the Horse at the Event
confirming the presence of Triamcinolone Acetonide constituted sufficient proof
of the violation of Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules;
▪ In any event, the APR did not dispute the presence of Triamcinolone Acetonide in
the Horse's Sample. Accordingly, the FEI respectfully submitted that it has
discharged its burden of establishing that the APR has violated Article 2.1 of the
ECM Rules;
▪ The FEI did not submit any request for the disqualification of results obtained by
the PR and Horse combination at the Event in this response as this was requested
in the procedure against the PR.
18. The FEI also submitted that Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules provided that a Person
Responsible with no previous ECM Rule violation, but who violated Article 2.1 of the ECM
1 The following section is a summary of the relevant facts and evidence of the Parties’ written submissions.
4

Rules, would be subject to a period of Ineligibility of six (6) months, unless they can rebut
the presumption of Fault on a balance of probability. 2
19. Therefore, in this case, to rebut the presumption of Fault, the APR must establish to the
satisfaction of the Tribunal (on a balance of probability), how the Triamcinolone Acetonide
entered the Horse’s system. The APR must also demonstrate one of the following:
▪ That he bears No Fault or Negligence for that occurrence, i.e., that he did not
know or suspect, and could not reasonably have known or suspected even with
the exercise of utmost caution, that he had administered to the horse (or the
horse’s system otherwise contained) a Prohibited Substance. If proven, the period
of Ineligibility is eliminated completely pursuant to Article 10.5 of the ECM Rules;
▪ That he bears No Significant Fault or Negligence for that occurrence, in which
case, the period of Ineligibility may be reduced based on the degree of fault,
pursuant to Article 10.6 of the ECM Rules;
20. The FEI submitted that If the APR failed to discharge this burden, the presumptive six-
month ban under Article 10.2 applies (subject to further increase based on prior
violations, Article 10.9 of the ECM Rules, or Aggravating Circumstances, Article 10.4 of the
ECM Rules).
21. The FEI noted that in respect of the ‘Threshold Requirement’, i.e., proving how
Triamcinolone Acetonide entered into the Horse's system, the ECM Rules stipulated, and
the jurisprudence of the FEI Tribunal and the CAS was very clear: It is a strict threshold
requirement of any plea of No (or No Significant) Fault or Negligence that the APR proves
how the Prohibited Substance entered into the Horse's system. Indeed, this requirement
must be strictly applied because without such proof it would be impossible to assess the
APR's degree of Fault or Negligence (or No Significant Fault or Negligence) for the presence
of the Controlled Medication Substances in the Horse.
2 The Preface to the EADCMRs specifies that 'in the discipline of Endurance, the registered Trainer shall be considered
as additional Person Responsible and held additionally responsible for any violation(s) under Articles 2.1 of the EAD Rules
and the ECM Rules.
This principle is further reflected in Article 118.3 of the FEI General Regulations (the GRs), which establishes that
'the Person Responsible shall be the Athlete who rides, vaults or drives the Horse during an Event, but the Owner and
other Support Personnel including but not limited to grooms and veterinarians may be regarded as additional Persons
Responsible if they are present at the Event or have made a relevant Decision about the Horse. In vaulting, the lunger
shall be an additional Person Responsible. In Endurance, the Trainer shall be the additional Person Responsible.'
Accordingly, under the applicable rules, the Trainer in Endurance is expressly designated as an Additional Person
Responsible, alongside the Person Responsible.
5

22. The FEI submitted in the latter context that the APR must provide clear and convincing
evidence that proved how the Triamcinolone Acetonide entered the Horse’s body. Taking
into consideration that the APR did not reply at all to the charges brought forward by the
FEI, the source of the Prohibited Substance was not established.
23. Consequently, the FEI respectfully submitted that the APR did not discharge his burden
of proof of establishing how Triamcinolone Acetonide entered the body of the Horse and
the “threshold requirement” was not fulfilled in this case.
24. The FEI noted that in respect of the Fault/Negligence for the Rule Violation, the starting
point of any evaluation was the “personal duty” of the APR following from Article 2.1.1 of
the ECM Rules, i.e., his personal duty to ensure that “no Controlled Medication Substance
is present in the Horse’s body during an Event without a valid Veterinary Form.” Further,
it was necessary to look at the definitions of Fault, as defined in Appendix 1 of the EADCM
Regulations.
‘Fault. Fault is any breach of duty or any lack of care appropriate to a particular situation.
Factors to be taken into consideration in assessing an Person Responsible and/or member of
the Support Personnel’s and/or other Person’s degree of Fault include, for example, the Person
Responsible’s and/or member of the Support Personnel’s and/or other Person’s experience,
whether the Person Responsible and/or member of the Support Personnel and/or other Person
is a Minor, special considerations such as impairment, the degree of risk that should have been
perceived by the Person Responsible and/or member of the Support Personnel and/or other
Person and the level of care and investigation exercised by the Person Responsible and/or
member of the Support Personnel and/or other Person in relation to what should have been
the perceived level of risk. In assessing the Person Responsible’s and/or member of the Support
Personnel’s and/or other Person’s degree of Fault, the circumstances considered must be
specific and relevant to explain the Person Responsible’s and/or member of the Support
Personnel’s and/or other Person’s departure from the expected standard of behaviour. Thus,
for example, the fact that the Person Responsible would lose the opportunity to earn large
sums of money during a period of Ineligibility, or the fact that the Person Responsible only has
a short time left in their career, or the timing of the sporting calendar, would not be relevant
factors to be considered in reducing the period of Ineligibility under Articles 10.6.1 or 10.6.2’.
‘No Fault or Negligence. The Persons Responsible and/or members of the Support Personnel
and/or other Persons establishing that they did not know or suspect, and could not reasonably
have known or suspected even with the exercise of utmost caution, that they had administered to
the Horse, or the Horse’s system otherwise contained, a Banned or Controlled Medication
Substance or they had Used on the Horse, a Banned or Controlled Medication Method or
otherwise violated an EAD or ECM Rule. Except in the case of a Minor, for any violation of Article
2.1, the Athlete must also establish how the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system’.
6

‘No Significant Fault or Negligence. The Person Responsible and/or member of the Support
Personnel establishing that their fault or negligence, when viewed in the totality of the
circumstances and taking into account the criteria for No Fault or Negligence, was not significant
in relationship to the EADCM Regulation violation. Except in the case of a Minor, for any violation
of Article 2.1 of the EAD Rules and Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules, the Person Responsible must also
establish how the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system’.’
25. As indicated in paragraph 22 of this Decision, the APR failed to establish how the
Controlled Medication Substance entered the Horse’s body, therefore it was not possible
to evaluate the APR’s level of (Significant) Fault or Negligence, if any, pursuant to the
applicable rules. Consequently, the FEI submitted that the presumption of Fault
established in Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules stands.
26. Accordingly, the FEI noted that no elimination or reduction of the period of Ineligibility
was possible in this case, and the minimum applicable sanction for the present violation
would be six (6) months of Ineligibility, in accordance with Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules.
Consequently, the presumption of Fault as stipulated in the Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules
remains.
a. The FEI respectfully requested that the Tribunal issue a decision:
(i) upholding the charge that the APR has violated Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules;
(ii) imposing a period of Ineligibility of six (6) months on the APR, commencing from
the date of the Final Decision in accordance with Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules;
(iii) fining the APR in the amount of 3’500 CHF;
(iv) ordering the APR to pay the legal costs of 2’000 CHF that the FEI has incurred in
these proceedings.
V. Legal Analysis
A. Jurisdiction
27. The Tribunal has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to Article 38 of the Statutes, Article
161 of the GRs, Article 8 of the ECM Rules and Article 18 of the IRs. The APR is a member
of the KSA-NF, which is a member of the FEI; therefore, the APR is bound by the ECM
Rules.
B. Legal Discussion
7

28. Although the Tribunal has fully considered all the facts, legal arguments and evidence in
the present proceedings, it refers only to the facts and evidence it considers necessary
to explain its reasoning in this decision.
i. The Burden of Proof
29. Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules states that sufficient proof of a violation is established by the
presence of a Controlled Medication Substance in a horse’s sample. The Tribunal is
satisfied that the laboratory report on the Sample reflects that the analytical tests were
performed in an acceptable manner and that the findings are accurate. The Tribunal is
further satisfied that the test results evidence the presence of Triamcinolone Acetonide
in the Sample taken from the Horse at the Event. Triamcinolone Acetonide is a Controlled
Medication Substance and the presence of this substance in a horse’s system is
prohibited under Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules.
30. Pursuant to Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules, the FEI bears the burden to establish all of the
elements of the ECM Rule violation to the comfortable satisfaction of the Tribunal. The
Tribunal notes that it is not in dispute that the FEI had successfully established that the
APR committed an ECM Rule violation. As a strict liability offence, it is not necessary to
prove intent, Fault, negligence or knowing Use.
31. The burden of proof then shifts to the APR. The standard of proof for the APR to establish
how the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system is by a balance of probability,
pursuant to Article 3.1 of the ECM Rules. It is not disputed by the Parties that for the APR
to escape a six (6) month sanction, he must establish, on a balance of probability: (i) how
the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system; and that (ii) he bears No
(Significant) Fault or Negligence pursuant to Articles 10.5 or 10.6 of the ECM Rules.
ii. Controlled Medication Rule Violation
32. As mentioned above, the violation of Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules is not in dispute. The
analysis of the Samples revealed the presence of Triamcinolone Acetonide in the Horse’s
system, which constitutes sufficient proof of the violation of Article 2.1. Therefore, the FEI
satisfied its burden to establish the ECM Rule violation and sufficiently proved the
objective elements of the violation pursuant to Article 3 of the ECM Rules.
iii. Elimination or Reduction of the Period of Ineligibility
33. Pursuant to Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules, the period of Ineligibility for an Article 2.1
8

violation is six (6) months, subject to a potential reduction for No (or No Significant) Fault
or Negligence in accordance with Articles 10.5 or 10.6 of the ECM Rules. To benefit from
a reduction, the APR must establish, as a threshold requirement, how the Prohibited
Substance entered the Horse’s system.3
34. The Panel notes from the evidence presented to date, the APR did not submit any
evidence establishing how the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system.
Therefore, the Tribunal finds that the APR did not discharge his burden of proving how
the Prohibited Substance entered the Horse’s system. The Tribunal therefore considers
that the source of the Prohibited Substance has not been established.
35. The starting point of any evaluation is the “personal duty” of the APR following from Article
2.1.1 of the ECM Rules, i.e., his personal duty to ensure that “no Controlled Medication
Substance is present in the Horse’s body during an Event without a valid Veterinary
Form.” It is the responsibility of the APR to rebut the presumption of Fault and to submit
all relevant arguments regarding the source of the Prohibited Substance, as well as any
allegations that he or she bears No (Significant) Fault or Negligence in relation to its
presence. In the present case, the APR has failed to respond to the charges brought
forward by the FEI. Consequently, the Tribunal finds that the APR is not entitled to any
reduction of the otherwise applicable period of Ineligibility under Articles 10.5 or 10.6 of
the ECM Rules.
iv. Sanctions
36. As the threshold criteria of source has not been proven, the Tribunal finds that the
applicable period of Ineligibility is six (6) months pursuant to Article 10.2 of the ECM Rules,
which shall commence on the date of notification of this decision.
37. The Tribunal also imposes a fine of CHF 3’500 on the PR and legal costs of CHF 2,000.
VI. Terms of the Decision
38. As a result, the Panel makes the following decision and imposes the following sanctions
in accordance with Article 164.11 of the GRs and Article 10 of the ECM Rules:
a) Mr WALEED violated Article 2.1 of the ECM Rules.
3 FEI Tribunal Decisions: C23-0031 [FEI 2023/FT12 – ALASOUF] dated 12 October 2023, C23-0034 [FEI 2023/CM05
– SAHM II] dated 8 September 2023, C23-0045 [FEI 2023/FT24 – DIFF LOOK] dated 2 November 2023, C23-0046
[2023/CM08 BALLON PARIS] dated 6 December 2023.
9

b) Mr WALEED is suspended for a period of six (6) months. The period of the Ineligibility
will be effective from the date of notification of this decision.
c) Mr WALEED is ordered to pay a fine of three thousand, five hundred Swiss Francs
(CHF 3’500).
d) Mr WALEED is ordered to pay the legal costs of two thousand Swiss Francs (CHF
2’000) that the FEI has incurred in these proceedings.
e) Mr WALEED, the Saudi NF and the FEI will be notified this Decision.
f) Mr WALEED may not, during the period of Ineligibility, participate in any capacity in a
Competition or activity that is authorised or organised by the FEI or any National
Federation or be present at an event (other than as a spectator) that is authorized
or organised by the FEI or any National Federation, or participate in any capacity in
Competitions authorised or organized by any international or national-level event
organisation (Article 10.13.1 of the ECM Rules).
g) If Mr WALEED violates any of the conditions in the previous paragraph during the
period of Ineligibility, the results of any such participation will be disqualified and a
new period of Ineligibility equal in length up to the original period of Ineligibility will
be added to the end of the original period of Ineligibility. In addition, further
sanctions may be imposed if appropriate (Article 10.13.3 of the ECM Rules).
h) According to Article 170 of the GRs, this Tribunal Decision is effective from the day
of written notification to the persons and bodies concerned.
VII. Legal Action
39. In accordance with Article 12 of the ECM Rules the Parties may appeal this Tribunal
Decision before the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) within twenty-one (21) days of
the present notification.
FOR THE TRIBUNAL
Ms Diane Pitts, Sole Panel Member

RENDERED BY THE FEI TRIBUNAL
29 June 2026
(OPERATIVE DECISION WITHDRAWING CHARGES ISSUED 21 MAY 2026)
In the matter of
FÉDÉRATION EQUESTRE INTERNATIONALE (the “FEI”)
